Topics.Title: What Is the Standards Library
Topics.Summary: Introduces the Standards Library as a reusable collection of academic standards built once and applied across multiple courses. Explains its purpose and its current 'System in Development' status as an evolving feature.

Elements.Title: Definition of the Standards Library
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Library is a reusable collection of academic standards that you build once and apply across multiple courses.
Elements.Notes: Think of it as a centralized repository rather than a per-course list — once assembled, the same library can serve many courses without rebuilding it each time.

Items.Text: The library stores academic standards in a single, organized location accessible across your courses.
Because it is built once and reused, it eliminates the need to re-enter or recreate standards for every new course you design.
The library is the foundation that makes standards mapping and coverage reporting possible.

Elements.Title: Purpose of the Standards Library
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Library exists to connect your course content to recognized academic standards, enabling systematic coverage tracking.
Elements.Notes: Without a library in place, there is no structured way to map topics or learning outcomes to standards, and therefore no way to generate meaningful coverage reports.

Items.Text: Its primary purpose is to give course designers a structured set of standards to map their topics and learning outcomes against.
By centralizing standards, the library makes coverage analysis consistent and comparable across courses.
The library supports accountability by creating a clear link between what is taught and the standards it addresses.

Elements.Title: AI-Assisted Assembly
Elements.BodyText: Rather than typing every standard by hand, you provide PreseMaker with a standards source and the AI extracts the standards into your library for you.
Elements.Notes: Acceptable sources include a web page URL from a standards site such as CPALMS, or text pasted directly from a standards document, as well as a plain-language description of the standards framework.

Items.Text: You supply either a URL pointing to a standards page, pasted text from a standards source, or a description of the standards framework.
The AI reads the material you provide and extracts individual standards, populating the library automatically.
After extraction, you review and save the standards before the library is ready for mapping.

Elements.Title: 'System in Development' Status
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Library is a newer capability currently labeled 'System in Development,' meaning it is an evolving feature whose requirements are still being finalized.
Elements.Notes: This label signals that workflows, interface elements, and specific behaviors may change as the feature matures. Instructors should expect refinements over time.

Items.Text: The 'System in Development' label indicates the feature is functional but not yet fully finalized.
Because requirements are still evolving, some aspects of the library's behavior or interface may change in future updates.
Users should treat current documentation as a working guide rather than a fixed specification.

Elements.Title: Reusability Across Courses
Elements.BodyText: One of the Standards Library's core advantages is that a single library can be mapped to multiple courses without being rebuilt each time.
Elements.Notes: This reusability is especially valuable for institutions or instructors who align many courses to the same standards framework, such as a state's K-12 standards.

Items.Text: Once a library is assembled and saved, it is available to use as the standards reference for any number of courses.
Reusability saves significant time compared to manually entering or verifying standards on a course-by-course basis.
Sharing one library across courses also ensures consistency in how standards are defined and labeled throughout an institution.

Topics.Title: Building the Library with AI
Topics.Summary: Covers how learners provide PreseMaker with a standards framework description, a web page URL, or pasted text from a standards source so the AI can extract and populate the library. Describes the review and save workflow after extraction.

Elements.Title: Providing Input to the AI
Elements.BodyText: To build a Standards Library, you give PreseMaker one of several types of input that the AI uses to identify and extract standards.
Elements.Notes: Acceptable inputs include a description of a standards framework by name, a URL pointing to a standards web page, or text pasted directly from a standards source such as a state site like CPALMS.

Items.Text: A framework description tells the AI which standards body or system to reference, even without a direct source document.
A URL or pasted text gives the AI an actual source to read, providing more reliable extraction than a name alone.
Pasting text is useful when a standards page cannot be accessed by URL or when you want to target a specific section of a larger document.

Elements.Title: How the AI Extracts Standards
Elements.BodyText: Once you provide input, PreseMaker's AI reads the material and extracts individual standards into your library automatically, rather than requiring you to enter each standard by hand.
Elements.Notes: This extraction process is the core time-saving feature of the Standards Library — it replaces manual data entry with AI-driven parsing of the source you supply.

Items.Text: The AI parses the input to identify discrete standards, including their codes and wording.
Extraction applies regardless of input type — framework description, URL, or pasted text — though accuracy varies by source quality.
Because this feature is still labeled 'System in Development,' extraction behavior and requirements may continue to evolve.

Elements.Title: Reviewing Extracted Standards
Elements.BodyText: After extraction, you review the standards the AI has populated before saving them to your library.
Elements.Notes: The review step is essential for catching errors, particularly for standards derived only from a framework description with no real source document to validate against.

Items.Text: Reviewing lets you confirm that codes and wording match what the official standards source actually states.
You can identify any standards that appear approximate or unfamiliar before they are saved and reused across courses.
The review step is especially important for Unverified standards, which may contain invented or approximate content.

Elements.Title: Saving Standards to the Library
Elements.BodyText: After reviewing the extracted standards, you save them to complete the library-building workflow, making the standards available for reuse across multiple courses.
Elements.Notes: Saving is the final step in the build workflow; once saved, the library can be mapped to course topics and learning outcomes without repeating the extraction process.

Items.Text: Saving locks in the extracted and reviewed standards as a reusable collection.
A saved library eliminates the need to re-enter or re-extract the same standards when working on different courses.
The build-once, reuse-often model is a primary efficiency benefit of the Standards Library feature.

Elements.Title: The Verified vs. Unverified Marker
Elements.BodyText: Each standard in the library is labeled either Verified or Unverified based on the source the AI used to produce it, not on the AI's confidence level.
Elements.Notes: This distinction is critical: Verified does not mean 'approved' or 'high confidence score,' and Unverified does not mean 'low confidence' — the marker indicates only whether a real source document was available during extraction.

Items.Text: Standards extracted from a URL or pasted text are marked Verified because they came from an actual source the AI could read.
Standards produced from only a framework name or description are marked Unverified because no real source was available to validate their codes and wording.
Unverified standards may be approximate or even invented by the AI, so you should check them against the official source before relying on them.
The Verified marker signals provenance — where the standard came from — not a percentage, confidence score, or pending-approval state.

Topics.Title: Understanding the Verified and Unverified Markers
Topics.Summary: Explains that the Verified marker indicates the provenance of a standard — whether it came from a real source provided by the user or was generated by the AI from a framework name alone. Clarifies that Unverified standards may contain approximate or invented codes and wording that must be checked against official sources.

Elements.Title: What the Verified/Unverified Marker Actually Means
Elements.BodyText: The Verified and Unverified markers indicate the provenance — the origin — of a standard, not a confidence score or approval status.
Elements.Notes: A common misconception is that the marker reflects how certain the AI is about the standard's accuracy. In reality, it only communicates where the standard came from.

Items.Text: Provenance refers to the source from which a standard was drawn, and that is the sole basis for the Verified or Unverified label.
The marker is not a percentage, a confidence rating, or a 'pending approval' indicator of any kind.
Understanding this distinction prevents misreading an Unverified standard as simply 'not yet approved' when it may actually contain inaccurate content.

Elements.Title: When a Standard Is Marked Verified
Elements.BodyText: A standard receives the Verified marker when it was extracted from a real source that you provided to the AI, such as a URL or pasted text from an official standards site.
Elements.Notes: For example, if you paste content from a state standards site like CPALMS or supply a direct web page address, the AI reads that material and extracts standards from it — those standards are marked Verified.

Items.Text: Verified standards are grounded in an actual document or page you supplied, so their codes and wording reflect what that source contained.
Providing a real source is the most reliable way to ensure the standards in your library match the official published versions.
Even Verified standards should be spot-checked, but they carry significantly less risk of containing invented or approximate content.

Elements.Title: When a Standard Is Marked Unverified
Elements.BodyText: A standard is marked Unverified when the AI generated it from a framework name alone, with no actual source document or web page provided for it to read.
Elements.Notes: For instance, if you simply name a standards framework without supplying a URL or pasted text, the AI will attempt to reconstruct the standards from its training knowledge — a process that can produce plausible-looking but inaccurate results.

Items.Text: Unverified standards may have approximate codes that look correct but do not match the official numbering system.
The wording of Unverified standards may be paraphrased, condensed, or even invented rather than taken verbatim from the official source.
The Unverified label is a direct signal that human review against the official source is required before these standards can be relied upon.

Elements.Title: Why Unverified Standards Can Contain Invented Content
Elements.BodyText: When an AI generates standards from a framework name without a source to read, it draws on its training data, which may be incomplete, outdated, or simply inaccurate for specific standard codes and language.
Elements.Notes: This is a known limitation of AI language models: they can produce output that is internally consistent and plausible in format while still being factually wrong in its specifics.

Items.Text: Standard codes in particular — alphanumeric identifiers like 'LAFS.3.RI.1.2' — are highly specific and easy for an AI to approximate incorrectly.
Official wording often contains precise legal or pedagogical language that an AI may paraphrase in ways that subtly change the meaning.
Treating Unverified standards as accurate without checking them could lead to mapping your course to standards that do not actually exist as described.

Elements.Title: How to Respond to Unverified Standards
Elements.BodyText: Because Unverified standards may be approximate or invented, the appropriate response is to verify each one against the official published source before using it in your course mapping.
Elements.Notes: Official sources include state department of education websites, standards body publications, and authoritative standards portals like CPALMS.

Items.Text: Locate the official source for the standards framework in question and compare each Unverified standard's code and wording against it.
If a standard's code or language does not match the official source, edit it in your Standards Library to reflect the correct information.
After verification, you can have confidence that your library accurately represents the framework, even if the standards initially arrived as Unverified.

Elements.Title: What the Marker Does Not Tell You
Elements.BodyText: It is important to understand the boundaries of what the Verified and Unverified markers communicate so you do not over- or under-rely on them.
Elements.Notes: Keeping the marker's meaning narrow and specific helps avoid both complacency with Verified standards and unnecessary distrust of the overall system.

Items.Text: The marker does not indicate how pedagogically appropriate a standard is for your course or learners.
Verified does not mean the standard is perfectly extracted — minor formatting or transcription issues can still occur — only that it came from a source you provided.
The marker is not a workflow state; it does not automatically change to Verified after you review an Unverified standard, so manual editing and judgment remain your responsibility.

Topics.Title: Cognitive Levels on Standards
Topics.Summary: Describes how each standard in the library can carry a Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive level. Explains how this level is later used by the Standards Coverage view to assess whether course content addresses a standard at the required depth.

Elements.Title: What Bloom's Taxonomy Cognitive Levels Represent
Elements.BodyText: Bloom's Taxonomy organizes cognitive learning into a hierarchy of levels, from basic recall up to complex evaluation and creation.
Elements.Notes: The six levels in ascending order are: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create. Each level represents a different depth of intellectual engagement with content.

Items.Text: Higher levels demand that learners do more than recall facts — they must manipulate, judge, or produce knowledge.
Assigning a cognitive level to a standard captures the depth at which a learner is expected to engage with that standard's content.
Different standards within the same framework may require very different cognitive depths, making level assignment essential for accurate coverage analysis.

Elements.Title: Assigning a Cognitive Level to a Standard in the Library
Elements.BodyText: Each standard stored in the Standards Library can carry a designated Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive level as one of its properties.
Elements.Notes: This assignment happens at the library-building stage, so the level travels with the standard whenever it is reused across courses.

Items.Text: The cognitive level is an attribute of the standard itself, not of the course content mapped to it.

When AI extracts standards from a source, a cognitive level may be suggested based on the language of the standard — verbs like 'recall' signal lower levels, while verbs like 'evaluate' signal higher ones.
You can review and adjust the assigned level to ensure it accurately reflects the intellectual demand stated in the official standard.

Elements.Title: How Cognitive Level Drives Depth Requirements
Elements.BodyText: The cognitive level attached to a standard sets a benchmark for how deeply course content must address that standard.
Elements.Notes: For example, a standard tagged at the 'Analyze' level means that simply presenting definitions in the course would not satisfy it — learners must be engaged in analysis.

Items.Text: A standard's cognitive level functions as a minimum depth requirement, not merely a label.
Course content that addresses the topic of a standard but at a lower cognitive level may be flagged as insufficient coverage.
This distinction ensures that coverage reporting reflects genuine instructional depth, not just subject-matter overlap.

Elements.Title: Role of Cognitive Level in the Standards Coverage View
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Coverage view uses each standard's cognitive level to assess whether mapped course content meets the standard at the required depth.
Elements.Notes: This means the coverage view performs a two-part check: does the course address the subject matter of the standard, and does it do so at or above the standard's cognitive level?

Items.Text: Coverage is considered adequate only when both the topic and the cognitive depth of the standard are addressed by course content.
A standard may appear mapped but still be flagged as insufficiently covered if the instructional activities or outcomes operate at a lower Bloom's level.
This capability allows instructors and designers to close depth gaps, not just content gaps, in their courses.

Elements.Title: Practical Implications of Getting the Cognitive Level Right
Elements.BodyText: Accurately assigning cognitive levels at the library stage is critical because errors will propagate into every course that maps to those standards.
Elements.Notes: Since the Standards Library is described as a system still in development, extra care in reviewing AI-suggested cognitive levels is advisable.

Items.Text: An underestimated cognitive level may cause the coverage view to pass content that does not actually meet the standard's full demand.
An overestimated cognitive level may flag well-designed content as insufficient, creating unnecessary revision work.
Checking the official wording of each standard — especially its action verbs — is the most reliable way to confirm the correct Bloom's level.

Topics.Title: Mapping Topics and Learning Outcomes to Standards
Topics.Summary: Walks through the process of linking a course's topics and learning outcomes to the relevant standards in the library. Explains how this mapping enables accurate standards coverage reporting across a course.

Elements.Title: What Mapping Means in the Standards Library
Elements.BodyText: Mapping is the process of linking your course's topics and learning outcomes to the relevant standards stored in your Standards Library.
Elements.Notes: Mapping is a deliberate, manual alignment step that happens after the library has been built. Without it, the system has no basis for generating coverage reports.

Items.Text: Each topic or learning outcome in your course can be connected to one or more standards from the library.
These connections are what tell the system which standards your course addresses and how.
Mapping is distinct from building the library — you must complete the library first, then perform the mapping step.

Elements.Title: Why Mapping Enables Standards Coverage Reporting
Elements.BodyText: The mapping between course content and standards is the foundation that makes accurate standards coverage reporting possible.
Elements.Notes: Without mapped connections, the system cannot determine which standards are taught, at what depth, or how many times across the course.

Items.Text: Once topics and learning outcomes are mapped, the Standards Coverage view can show which standards are addressed and which are missing.
Coverage reporting draws entirely from the mapped relationships — no mapping means no reportable coverage.
This allows educators and administrators to see at a glance where gaps or overlaps exist across the full course.

Elements.Title: Mapping Topics to Standards
Elements.BodyText: Individual course topics can be linked directly to one or more standards in the library to indicate which standards that topic addresses.
Elements.Notes: A single topic may map to multiple standards, and a single standard may be addressed by multiple topics throughout the course.

Items.Text: Navigate to a course topic and select the relevant standards from your library to create the association.
Mapping a topic signals that instruction on that topic contributes to learner mastery of the linked standard.
Reviewing topic-level mappings helps ensure every major instructional area is connected to at least one standard.

Elements.Title: Mapping Learning Outcomes to Standards
Elements.BodyText: Learning outcomes can also be mapped to standards, providing a more precise alignment between what learners are expected to demonstrate and the standard being addressed.
Elements.Notes: Outcome-level mapping is especially useful when cognitive depth matters, since outcomes often specify the level of mastery expected.

Items.Text: A learning outcome describes a specific, measurable result of instruction and can be tied directly to the standard it fulfills.
Mapping at the outcome level offers finer granularity than topic-level mapping alone, supporting more detailed coverage analysis.
When a standard carries a Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive level, the mapped outcome's depth can be compared to confirm the standard is taught at the required level.

Elements.Title: Using Cognitive Level in the Mapping Process
Elements.BodyText: Standards in the library can carry a Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive level, and this level plays a role in how the coverage view evaluates your mapped content.
Elements.Notes: For example, a standard requiring 'Evaluate' (a higher-order level) would not be fully satisfied by a learning outcome written only at the 'Remember' level.

Items.Text: When you map a learning outcome to a standard that has a cognitive level assigned, the system can check whether the outcome meets that depth.
This helps instructors identify cases where a standard is technically covered but not taught at the rigor the standard demands.
Attending to cognitive level during mapping improves the quality and defensibility of your standards alignment.

Elements.Title: Reviewing and Confirming Your Mappings
Elements.BodyText: After mapping topics and outcomes to standards, reviewing the full set of connections ensures completeness and accuracy before relying on coverage reports.
Elements.Notes: This review step is particularly important for Unverified standards, whose wording or codes may be approximate and should be checked against the official source.

Items.Text: Scan all mapped standards to confirm each connection accurately reflects what the topic or outcome actually teaches.
Look for standards in your library that have no mappings, as these represent potential gaps in your course's coverage.
Correcting or adding mappings at this stage ensures the coverage report reflects the true state of your course alignment.
